I always forget.~~ Everything in RLP is a byte array or a list, so this statement doesn't make sense. It should just be a `0` byte or a `1` byte I believe. ~~Oh, actually 0x80 may be a special case in Ethereum's pre-RLP encoding step...~~ Also wrong. I'm pretty sure `yParity` should always be 0 byte or 1 byte after RLP encoding. Ok, that's what I thought. So it ends up as `00` or `01`, correct? 0x80 is a 0-length byte array. Oh, but Ethereum is dumb. `The integer 0 = [ 0x80 ]` 😖 `The encoded integer 0 (’\x00’) = [ 0x00 ]` What does that even mean?! I'm looking at the same page as you and I am confounded haha (I have been over this a dozen times over the years, and even written an RLP encoder and decoder and *every* time I am confused. Glad I'm not the only one haha. I think in this case, since it's never going to need more than 1 byte to encode, we go with `00`, `01` ``` def to_binary(x): if x == 0: return '' else: return to_binary(int(x / 256)) + chr(x % 256) ``` Pretty sure the protocol just straight up special cases `0` for some reason. > positive RLP integers must be represented in big endian binary form with no leading zeroes (**thus making the integer value zero be equivalent to the empty byte array**). It is a side effect of the zero stripping that happens prior to RLP encoding. When you strip all of the leading zeros off of `0`, you get null. I see, so `80` and `01` then? If you want to keep your code clean, that should happen *prior* to RLP. Since RLP (the encoding system) *only* knows how to encode byte arrays and lists. It doesn't have any concept of numbers. Ethereum has an un-named encoding scheme for turning various types of data into byte arrays and lists that it applies to things prior to RLP encoding them. In the RLP document it says: > encoding specific data types (eg. strings, floats) is left up to higher-order protocols And then literally the next words are: > but positive RLP integers must be represented in big endian binary form with no leading zeroes So that is the "higher level protocol". 😬 <@!213672586264051717> as for that receipt-root, this is the encoded receipt, itself. Which is later placed into a trie for producing the root. I suspect the root of our mismatch should be here. `` Ah. Oh. Yeah this is my bad. I'll update them tomorrow, but it's due to a different hasher being used, not based on the trie 🙂 No worries!
